chapters.title: The Last Day
paragraphs: ECHECRATES: Were you there in person, Phaedo — in the prison with Socrates on the day he drank the poison?
PHAEDO: Yes, Echecrates, I was.

ECHECRATES: I'd love to hear about his death. What did he say in his last hours? We heard he died by poison, but no one knew any details. No one from Phlius goes to Athens anymore, and it's been ages since anyone from Athens has visited us — so we've had no clear account.
PHAEDO: You didn't hear about the trial?
ECHECRATES: Someone told us about the trial, but we couldn't understand why, after being condemned, he wasn't executed right away — why there was such a long delay. What was the reason?
PHAEDO: It was coincidence, Echecrates. The day before his trial, the stern of the ship that Athens sends to Delos happened to have been crowned.
ECHECRATES: What ship is that?

PHAEDO: It's the ship in which, according to Athenian tradition, Theseus sailed to Crete with the fourteen young people — he saved them and himself. They say the Athenians vowed to Apollo that if they were saved, they would send a yearly mission to Delos. This custom continues to this day. The entire period of the voyage — from the moment the priest crowns the ship's stern until it returns — is considered holy, and during that time no public executions may take place. When contrary winds delay the ship, the voyage can take quite a while. The ship happened to be crowned the day before the trial, which is why Socrates was held in prison so long after his condemnation.
ECHECRATES: What was the manner of his death, Phaedo? What was said and done? Which of his friends were with him? Or did the authorities forbid visitors — so that he died alone?
PHAEDO: No, several friends were with him.
ECHECRATES: If you have the time, I wish you would tell me everything that happened, as exactly as you can.
PHAEDO: I have nothing else to do, and I'll try my best. Being reminded of Socrates is always the greatest pleasure to me, whether I'm speaking about him or listening to someone else do so.
ECHECRATES: Your listeners feel the same way. Please be as detailed as you can.

PHAEDO: I had a strange feeling that day. I could hardly believe I was witnessing a friend's death, and so I felt no pity for him, Echecrates. He died so fearlessly, and his words and manner were so noble and gracious, that he seemed blessed to me. I thought he couldn't be going to the other world without divine guidance, and that he would be happy there, if anyone ever was. So I didn't pity him as you might expect. But I didn't feel the usual pleasure I take in philosophical discussion either — though philosophy was our subject. There was pleasure, but mixed with a strange undercurrent of pain, knowing he would soon die. We all felt this double sensation — laughing and weeping by turns, especially the excitable Apollodorus. You know the type?
ECHECRATES: Yes.
PHAEDO: He was completely beside himself. And all of us were deeply moved.
ECHECRATES: Who was present?

PHAEDO: Among the native Athenians: Apollodorus, Critobulus and his father Crito, Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, Antisthenes; also Ctesippus from Paeania, Menexenus, and a few others. Plato, I believe, was ill.
ECHECRATES: Were there any visitors from other cities?
PHAEDO: Yes — Simmias, Cebes, and Phaedondes from Thebes; and Euclid and Terpison from Megara.
ECHECRATES: What about Aristippus and Cleombrotus?
PHAEDO: No, they were reportedly in Aegina.
ECHECRATES: Anyone else?
PHAEDO: I think that was nearly everyone.
ECHECRATES: And what did you talk about?

PHAEDO: I'll start from the beginning and try to recount the whole conversation. In the days before, we'd been meeting early each morning at the courthouse near the prison, waiting for the doors to open — they didn't open very early — and then spending the day with Socrates. On this last morning, we gathered earlier than usual, having heard the evening before that the sacred ship had returned from Delos. We arranged to meet very early at the usual spot. When we arrived, the guard who answered the door came out and told us to wait. 'The Eleven are with Socrates now,' he said. 'They're removing his chains and informing him that he is to die today.' He returned shortly and let us in. We found Socrates just freed from his chains, with Xanthippe — you know her — sitting beside him, holding their child. When she saw us, she cried out: 'Oh, Socrates, this is the last time you will talk with your friends, or they with you!' Socrates turned to Crito and said, 'Crito, have someone take her home.' Some of Crito's people led her away, crying and beating her breast.

When she was gone, Socrates sat up on the couch, bent his leg, and rubbed it. 'How strange,' he said, 'is this thing called pleasure, and how curiously it's related to pain — which you'd think was its opposite. They never appear together at the same moment, yet whoever pursues one is almost always forced to take the other too. They have two bodies but are joined at the head. If Aesop had thought of them, I think he would have written a fable about God trying to reconcile their quarrel, and when he couldn't, fastening their heads together. That's why when one arrives, the other follows — as I'm experiencing right now. The chain caused pain in my leg, and now that it's gone, pleasure comes right behind.'

Cebes said: 'I'm glad you mentioned Aesop, Socrates. It reminds me of a question many people have asked — Evenus the poet asked me just the other day, and he's sure to ask again — why you, who never wrote a line of poetry before, have been turning Aesop's fables into verse now that you're in prison, and also composing a hymn to Apollo.'

'Tell him the truth, Cebes,' he replied. 'I had no intention of competing with him or his poems — I knew that would be no easy task. I just wanted to clear up a doubt about certain dreams I've had throughout my life. The same dream has come to me in different forms, but always saying the same thing: "Make music, Socrates." I'd always assumed this meant philosophy — the noblest and best kind of music, which I was already pursuing. The dream was just encouraging me, like spectators cheering a runner who's already running. But I wasn't entirely sure. Maybe it meant music in the ordinary sense. Since I'm under a death sentence and the festival gave me a reprieve, I thought it safest to satisfy the scruple and compose some verses before I go.'

'First I wrote a hymn to the god of the festival. Then, realizing that a true poet should create stories rather than just arrange words — and that I have no gift for invention — I took some of Aesop's fables that I knew by heart, the first ones that came to mind, and turned them into verse. Tell Evenus this, Cebes, and wish him well. Tell him I'd advise him to follow me as soon as he can, if he's a wise man. It seems I'll be leaving today — the Athenians have decided.'
Simmias said: 'What a strange message for Evenus! From what I know of him, he won't willingly take your advice.'
'Why not?' said Socrates. 'Isn't Evenus a philosopher?'
'I think he is,' said Simmias.
'Then he — or anyone with a philosophical spirit — will be willing to die. But he won't take his own life, because that is considered wrong.'
Here Socrates shifted position, putting his feet on the ground, and sat like that for the rest of the conversation.
'Why do you say,' asked Cebes, 'that it's wrong to take your own life, but that a philosopher should be willing to follow someone who is dying?'
Socrates replied: 'Haven't you and Simmias — as students of Philolaus — heard him speak about this?'
'Yes, but what he said was obscure, Socrates.'

'My own words are just an echo of what I've heard. But there's no reason I shouldn't repeat it. Indeed, since I'm about to journey to another place, what better way to spend the time between now and sunset than thinking and talking about the nature of that journey?'

'Then tell me, Socrates, why is suicide considered wrong? I've certainly heard Philolaus say so, when he was staying with us in Thebes, and others have said the same — but I've never understood what any of them meant.'

'Don't lose heart,' replied Socrates. 'The day may come when you understand. I suppose you wonder why, when other evils can sometimes be good for certain people at certain times, death alone is the exception — why a man who would be better off dead is not permitted to do himself this service, but must wait for someone else to do it.'
'Exactly,' said Cebes, laughing gently in his Boeotian accent.

'I admit it looks inconsistent, but there may be no real contradiction. There's a teaching, passed along in secret, that we humans are like prisoners who have no right to break out and escape. This is a deep mystery I don't fully understand. But I do believe that the gods are our guardians and that we belong to them. Don't you agree?'
'Yes, absolutely,' said Cebes.
'And if one of your own possessions — an ox or a donkey — decided on its own to die, without your permission, wouldn't you be furious? Wouldn't you punish it if you could?'
'Of course,' replied Cebes.
'Then perhaps there's good reason to say that a person should wait and not take his own life until God calls him — as God is now calling me.'

'Yes, Socrates, there seems to be truth in that. And yet, how can you reconcile this — that we belong to the gods, who are the best possible guardians — with the philosopher's willingness to die? It makes no sense that the wisest people should happily leave a service where they're looked after by the best masters. Surely no wise person thinks they can take better care of themselves than the gods take of them. A fool might think so — might argue he should escape his master. But the wise person would want to stay forever with someone better than themselves. So on this view, the wise should grieve at death, and the foolish should rejoice — the opposite of what you said.'
Cebes' earnestness seemed to please Socrates. 'Here,' he said, turning to us, 'is a man who's always questioning and never easily convinced by the first argument he hears.'

'And I must say,' added Simmias, 'Cebes' objection seems to have some force. Why would a truly wise person want to flee from a master better than himself? I think Cebes is really aiming at you, Socrates — he thinks you're too ready to leave us and too ready to leave the gods, whom you call our good masters.'
'Fair enough,' replied Socrates. 'You think I should defend myself as if I were on trial?'
'We'd like that,' said Simmias.

'Then let me try to make a better defense before you than I did before the judges. I'll freely admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I should grieve at death — if I weren't persuaded, first, that I'm going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I'm as certain as I can be of anything), and second — though I'm less sure of this — to departed souls who are better than the ones I'm leaving behind. So I don't grieve as I might, because I have good hope that something remains for the dead, and as has been said since ancient times, something far better for the good than for the evil.'

'But will you take these thoughts with you and not share them with us, Socrates?' said Simmias. 'We have a right to share in this benefit too. And if you can convince us, that will answer the charge against you.'
'I'll try my best,' replied Socrates. 'But first let me hear what Crito wants — he's been trying to say something for a while.'

'Just this, Socrates,' said Crito. 'The man who's going to give you the poison asked me to tell you not to talk too much. He says talking generates heat, and heat can interfere with the poison. People who get themselves worked up sometimes have to take a second or even a third dose.'
'Tell him to mind his own business,' said Socrates, 'and to prepare two or three doses if necessary. That's all.'
'I knew you'd say that,' replied Crito, 'but he kept insisting.'
'Never mind him,' said Socrates.

'And now, my friends, I want to explain to you why I believe a true philosopher has good reason to be cheerful when facing death, and may hope to find the greatest good in the world to come. Let me try to show you, Simmias and Cebes. The true devotee of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by others. They don't realize that he is always pursuing death and dying. If this is so — if he has desired death his whole life — why should he complain when the time finally comes for what he has always sought?'

Simmias laughed: 'You've made me laugh, Socrates, though I'm not in a laughing mood. I can't help thinking that most people, hearing this, would say you've described philosophers perfectly — and our countrymen back home would agree that the life philosophers want is really death, and that they've caught them out at last, deserving the death they desire.'

chapters.title: The Philosopher and Death
paragraphs: And they're right, Simmias — except for the part about 'catching us out.' They haven't actually understood what kind of death the true philosopher deserves, or how he deserves and desires it. But forget about them — let's discuss this among ourselves. Do we believe there is such a thing as death?
'Certainly,' replied Simmias.

'Isn't death the separation of soul from body? To be dead means that the body exists on its own, released from the soul, and the soul exists on her own, released from the body. Death is nothing other than this?'
'Exactly,' he replied.
'Here's another question that may shed light on our inquiry: Should the philosopher care about the pleasures — if you can call them pleasures — of eating and drinking?'
'Certainly not,' answered Simmias.
'What about the pleasures of love — should he care about those?'
'Not at all.'
'And what about other ways of indulging the body — expensive clothing, sandals, other physical adornments? Doesn't the philosopher despise anything beyond what nature requires?'
'I'd say the true philosopher would despise them.'
'So wouldn't you say that the philosopher is entirely concerned with the soul, not the body? He wants, as far as possible, to free himself from the body and turn toward the soul?'
'Yes, absolutely.'
'In these matters, philosophers — more than anyone — can be seen separating the soul from the body's influence.'
'Very true.'
'Meanwhile, Simmias, the rest of the world thinks that a person who takes no pleasure in bodily things isn't really living — that someone indifferent to such pleasures might as well be dead.'
'That's also true.'

'Now, what about the pursuit of knowledge? Is the body a help or a hindrance? I mean: do sight and hearing contain any truth? Aren't they — as the poets are always telling us — unreliable witnesses? And if even the best of our senses are inaccurate, what about the rest?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'Then when does the soul reach the truth? Clearly, whenever she tries to investigate anything alongside the body, she's deceived.'
'True.'
'So true reality must be grasped by thought alone, if it can be grasped at all?'
'Yes.'

'And thought works best when the mind gathers into herself, undisturbed by sounds, sights, pain, or pleasure — when she takes leave of the body and has as little to do with it as possible, reaching toward pure being without bodily sense or desire?'
'Certainly.'
'And in this, the philosopher dishonors the body — his soul flees from it and longs to be alone?'
'That's true.'
'Now, Simmias — is there such a thing as absolute justice?'
'Without a doubt.'
'And absolute beauty? And absolute good?'
'Of course.'
'But have you ever seen any of these things with your eyes?'
'Certainly not.'

'Have you ever perceived them through any bodily sense? I'm talking not just about these, but about absolute greatness, health, strength — the true essence of everything. Has their reality ever been perceived through bodily organs? Or does the closest approach to knowing their true nature come from ordering your mental vision so precisely that you grasp the exact essence of each thing you contemplate?'
'Certainly.'

'And the person who achieves the purest knowledge goes to each thing with the mind alone — not introducing sight or any other sense alongside reason, but using the pure light of the mind to search into the pure truth of each thing. The person who has rid themselves, as far as possible, of eyes, ears, and the entire body — which in their view are distracting elements that corrupt the soul and prevent her from attaining truth and knowledge — if not such a person, who will attain knowledge of true being?'
'What you say has wonderful truth in it, Socrates,' replied Simmias.

'And when genuine philosophers consider all this, won't they say something like: "Haven't we found a line of thought that leads to this conclusion — that while we're in the body, and the soul is contaminated with the body's evils, we'll never fully attain what we desire, which is truth? The body is an endless source of trouble: it demands food; it falls prey to diseases that interrupt our search for truth; it fills us with desires, fears, fantasies of every kind, and endless foolishness — so much so that, as people say, it robs us of the very power of thought. Where do wars and conflicts come from? From the body and its desires. Wars are caused by the love of money, and money must be acquired for the body's sake. Because of all this, we have no time for philosophy. And worst of all — even when we're free and turn to serious thinking, the body keeps intruding, causing chaos in our inquiries, dazzling us so we can't see the truth.',

'It has been proven by experience that if we want pure knowledge, we must be free of the body — the soul must behold things as they truly are, by herself. Only then will we attain the wisdom we claim to love — not in life, but after death. For if the soul can't have pure knowledge while attached to the body, then either knowledge can't be attained at all, or only after death — when the soul is finally separated from the body and exists on her own. In this present life, we come closest to knowledge when we have the least possible contact with the body, keeping ourselves pure until God is pleased to release us. Having rid ourselves of the body's foolishness, we shall be pure and converse with the pure, and know the clear light everywhere — which is nothing other than the light of truth. The impure are not permitted to approach the pure." These are the kinds of things, Simmias, that true lovers of knowledge can't help saying to each other. Don't you agree?'
'Without a doubt, Socrates.'

'But if this is true, my friend, there's great reason to hope that where I'm going — when I reach the end of my journey — I'll finally attain what I've pursued my whole life. So I go on my way rejoicing, and so should every person who believes their mind has been prepared and purified.'
'Certainly,' replied Simmias.

'And what is purification but the separation of soul from body, as I was saying? The habit of the soul gathering herself from all parts of the body into herself — dwelling in her own place alone, both in this life and the next, as far as she can? The release of the soul from the chains of the body?'
'Very true,' he said.
'And this separation and release of the soul from the body is called death?'
'Exactly,' he said.
'And true philosophers — they alone — are always seeking to release the soul. Isn't the separation and release of the soul from the body their special study?'
'That is true.'
'And as I was saying at first, it would be absurd for people who have practiced living as close to death as possible to complain when death actually arrives.'
'Clearly.'

'True philosophers, Simmias, are always practicing dying. Death is less terrible to them than to anyone else. Think about it: if they've been the body's enemy in every way, wanting only to be alone with the soul — when this wish is granted, how contradictory it would be to tremble and complain, instead of rejoicing at departing to a place where they hope to find what they've desired all their lives — wisdom — and to be rid of the companion they've despised. Many people have willingly gone to the underworld, drawn by the hope of seeing a loved one there. Won't a true lover of wisdom — deeply convinced that only in the next world can he enjoy wisdom in her purity — depart with joy? Surely he will, my friend, if he's a true philosopher. He'll be firmly convinced that there, and only there, can wisdom be found in her pure form. If this is true, it would be utterly absurd to fear death.'
'It would indeed,' replied Simmias.
'And when you see a man who dreads the approach of death, isn't that proof enough that he's not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body — and probably of money or power, or both?'
'Quite so,' he replied.
'And isn't courage, Simmias, a quality that especially belongs to the philosopher?'
'Certainly.'

'And temperance — which even ordinary people understand as control over the passions and superiority to them — isn't temperance a virtue belonging only to those who despise the body and live for philosophy?'
'Absolutely.'
'Because the courage and temperance of other people, if you think about it, are actually self-contradictory.'
'How so?'
'Well,' he said, 'you know that most people consider death a terrible evil.'
'Very true,' he said.
'And don't courageous people face death only because they fear something worse?'
'That's true.'
'So everyone except philosophers is courageous only out of fear — courageous because they're cowards. A strange kind of courage.'
'Very true.'

'And isn't it the same with temperance? People are temperate because they're intemperate — which sounds like a contradiction, but that's exactly how this foolish temperance works. They're afraid of losing certain pleasures, so they abstain from others because they're overwhelmed by the first ones. Being conquered by pleasure is called intemperance, yet their version of "conquering pleasure" actually means being conquered by a different pleasure. That's what I mean when I say they're made temperate through intemperance.'
'So it seems.'

'But trading one fear or pleasure or pain for another — greater for lesser, as if they were coins — is not the exchange of true virtue. There is only one true currency, Simmias, for which all things should be traded: wisdom. Only in exchange for wisdom, and in company with wisdom, is anything truly bought or sold — whether courage, temperance, or justice. All true virtue is wisdom's companion, regardless of what pleasures or pains or fears may accompany her. But virtue assembled from such things, traded back and forth without wisdom, is merely the shadow of virtue — with no real freedom, health, or truth in it. True virtue is the purification from all these things, and temperance, justice, courage, and wisdom herself are the means of purification. The founders of the Mystery rites seem to have had a real meaning when they said, in their symbolic way, that whoever enters the underworld unpurified will lie in the muck, while the purified will dwell with the gods.'

'For "many carry the thyrsus," as they say in the Mysteries, "but few are truly initiated" — meaning, as I understand it, few are true philosophers. I have spent my whole life trying to be counted among them. Whether I've succeeded, I'll know for certain in a little while, God willing, when I arrive in the other world. This is my belief. So I maintain, Simmias and Cebes, that I'm right not to grieve at leaving you and my masters in this world, because I believe I'll find equally good masters and friends in the next. Most people don't believe this — so if I can make a more convincing case to you than I did to my Athenian judges, that will be well.'

Cebes replied: 'I agree with most of what you say, Socrates. But when it comes to the soul, people tend to be skeptical. They fear that when the soul leaves the body, she goes nowhere — that on the very day of death she perishes and dissolves like smoke or vapor, vanishing into nothing the moment she's released. If the soul could gather herself together after escaping the evils you've described, there would be good reason to hope you're right. But proving that the soul continues to exist after death, with any force or intelligence — that requires a great deal of argument and evidence.'
'True, Cebes,' said Socrates. 'Shall I suggest we discuss the probabilities of these things?'
'I'd very much like to hear your views about them,' said Cebes.

'I don't think,' said Socrates, 'that anyone hearing me now — not even one of my old enemies, the comic poets — could accuse me of idle chatter about things that don't concern me. So if you're willing, let's proceed with the inquiry.'

chapters.title: The Argument from Opposites
paragraphs: 'Let's consider whether the souls of the dead exist in the underworld. There's an ancient doctrine that says souls go from here to the other world, and return from there to be born again among the living. If it's true that the living come from the dead, then our souls must exist in that other world — otherwise, how could they be born again? This would be conclusive if we could prove that the living really do come only from the dead. But if not, we'll need other arguments.'
'Very true,' replied Cebes.

'Then let's examine the question broadly — not just about humans, but about animals, plants, and everything that is generated. The proof will be easier that way. Isn't everything that has an opposite generated from its opposite? Good and evil, just and unjust — there are countless such pairs. I want to show that in all opposites, there's necessarily an alternation: for instance, whatever becomes greater must first have been less.'
'True.'
'And what becomes less must once have been greater.'
'Yes.'
'And the weaker comes from the stronger, and the faster from the slower.'
'Very true.'
'And the worse from the better, and the more just from the more unjust.'
'Of course.'
'Is this true of all opposites? Are we satisfied that everything is generated from its opposite?'
'Yes.'

'And in this universal opposition, aren't there always two processes going back and forth between the opposites? Where there's a greater and a lesser, there's also a process of increase and decrease — what grows is said to wax, what decays to wane?'
'Yes,' he said.

'And there are many other processes — division and composition, cooling and heating — that equally involve passage from one opposite to the other. Even when we don't always name them, all opposites are truly generated from one another, with a process connecting them?'
'Very true,' he replied.
'Well, isn't there an opposite of life, just as sleep is the opposite of waking?'
'True,' he said.
'And what is it?'
'Death,' he answered.
'And if these are opposites, they must be generated from one another, with their own intermediate processes?'
'Of course.'

'Now,' said Socrates, 'I'll analyze one of these pairs — sleep and waking — and you can analyze the other for me. Sleep is opposed to waking. From sleeping, waking is generated; from waking, sleeping. The process of generation is in one case falling asleep, in the other waking up. Agreed?'
'Entirely.'
'Then analyze life and death the same way. Isn't death opposed to life?'
'Yes.'
'And they are generated from one another?'
'Yes.'
'What is generated from the living?'
'The dead.'
'And what from the dead?'
'I can only say — the living.'
'Then living things — whether people or anything else — are generated from the dead?'
'That's clear,' he replied.
'Then it follows that our souls exist in the underworld?'
'That is true.'
'And one of the two processes is visible — the act of dying is certainly visible?'
'Certainly,' he said.
'What follows? Shall we deny the opposite process? Shall we imagine that nature walks on one leg? Mustn't we assign to death a corresponding process of generation?'
'We must,' he replied.
'And what is that process?'
'Return to life.'
'And return to life, if such a thing exists, is the birth of the dead into the world of the living?'
'Exactly.'

'So here's a new argument proving that the living come from the dead, just as the dead come from the living. If this is true, it's strong evidence that the souls of the dead exist somewhere, from which they return.'
'Yes, Socrates,' he said. 'The conclusion seems to follow necessarily from what we've agreed.'

'And our admissions were fair, Cebes, as I can show. If generation only went in one direction, with no returning cycle in nature — no turning back of elements into their opposites — then everything would eventually end up in the same state, and there would be no more generation.'
'What do you mean?' he said.

'Simple enough. If there were no alternation of sleeping and waking, the story of Endymion's eternal sleep would become meaningless — everything else would be asleep too, and he'd be indistinguishable. If there were only composition and no division, the chaos Anaxagoras described would return. In the same way, dear Cebes, if everything that lives were to die and stay dead — never coming back to life — wouldn't everything eventually be dead, with nothing left alive? If the living spring from something other than the dead, and then they too die, mustn't everything ultimately be swallowed up in death?'
'There's no escape from that, Socrates,' said Cebes. 'Your argument seems absolutely true.'

'Yes, Cebes, it is and must be so, in my view. We haven't been deceived in our reasoning. I'm confident that there truly is such a thing as living again — that the living spring from the dead, that the souls of the dead exist, and that good souls fare better than evil ones.'

chapters.title: The Argument from Recollection
paragraphs: Cebes added: 'Your favorite doctrine, Socrates — that knowledge is simply recollection — if true, also necessarily implies that we existed before this life and learned then what we now recall. But this would be impossible unless our soul existed somewhere before taking human form. Here's another proof of the soul's immortality.'
'But tell me, Cebes,' said Simmias, interrupting, 'what are the arguments for this recollection doctrine? I'm not sure I remember them at the moment.'

'One excellent proof,' said Cebes, 'comes from questioning. If you ask someone the right questions, they can arrive at the correct answer by themselves. How could they do this unless they already possessed knowledge and right reason? This is most clearly demonstrated with geometric diagrams and such things.'
'But if you're still skeptical, Simmias,' said Socrates, 'perhaps you'll agree when you look at it from another angle — that is, if you still doubt that knowledge is recollection.'
'I'm not really skeptical,' said Simmias. 'I just need the doctrine recalled to my own memory. What Cebes said is already bringing it back. But I'd still like to hear what you were about to say.'
'Here's what I mean,' he replied. 'We'd agree that whatever a person recollects, they must have known at some earlier time.'
'Very true.'

'And what is the nature of this knowledge or recollection? What I mean is: when a person perceives something — by seeing, hearing, or any other sense — and this perception leads them to think of something else that isn't the same kind of knowledge but different — can't we fairly say they're recollecting that second thing?'
'What do you mean?'
'Let me illustrate. Knowing a lyre isn't the same as knowing a person, is it?'
'True.'

'Yet when lovers see a lyre, a garment, or anything else their beloved has used, don't they instantly picture the beloved in their mind? From knowing the lyre, they form an image of the person it belongs to. That is recollection. Similarly, seeing Simmias might remind you of Cebes — and there are endless such examples.'
'Endless, indeed,' replied Simmias.
'And recollection most often means recovering something that was forgotten through the passage of time or inattention.'
'Very true,' he said.
'Now — can't seeing a picture of a horse or a lyre make you think of a person? And can't a picture of Simmias remind you of Cebes?'
'True.'
'Or lead you to recall Simmias himself?'
'Certainly.'
'And in all these cases, isn't recollection triggered both by similar things and by dissimilar things?'
'It is.'
'And when recollection comes from similar things, don't we naturally ask whether this thing falls short of the one we're remembering — whether it's less perfect in its similarity?'
'Certainly,' he said.

chapters.title: The Affinity Argument
paragraphs: And shall we go one step further and affirm that there is such a thing as equality itself—not the equality of one piece of wood or stone with another, but over and above those, an absolute equality? Shall we say so?
Say so, yes, Simmias replied, and swear to it with all the confidence in the world.
And do we know the nature of this absolute essence?
To be sure, he said.

And where did we get that knowledge? Didn't we see equalities in material things—pieces of wood and stones and the like—and from those gather the idea of an equality that is different from them? You'll grant there's a difference. Or look at it another way: don't the very same pieces of wood or stone appear equal at one time and unequal at another?
That's certainly true.
But are things that are truly equal ever unequal? Or is the idea of equality the same as that of inequality?
Impossible, Socrates.
Then these so-called equals are not the same as the idea of equality itself?
Clearly not, Socrates.
And yet from these equals, different as they are from the idea of equality, you conceived that idea and reached it?
Very true, he said.
An idea which might be either like them or unlike them?
Yes.
But that makes no difference. Whenever from seeing one thing you conceive another—whether like or unlike—there must surely have been an act of recollection?
Very true.

Now what would you say about equal pieces of wood and stone, or other material equals? What impression do they make? Are they equal in the same sense in which absolute equality is equal? Or do they fall short of that perfect equality in some measure?
Yes, he said, and by a very great measure too.

And must we not grant this: when someone looks at an object and notices that it aims at being another thing, but falls short of it and cannot be that other thing, but is inferior to it—whoever makes this observation must have had previous knowledge of that thing to which the other, though similar, was inferior?
Certainly.
And hasn't this been our own case with equals and absolute equality?
Precisely.
Then we must have known equality before the time when we first saw material equals and reflected that all these apparent equals strive to reach absolute equality but fall short of it?
Very true.
And we also recognize that this absolute equality is known, and can only be known, through sight or touch or some other of the senses, which are all alike in this respect?
Yes, Socrates, as far as the argument is concerned, one sense is as good as another.
So it is from the senses that we derive the knowledge that all sensible things aim at an absolute equality which they fall short of?
Yes.

Then before we began to see or hear or perceive in any way, we must have had knowledge of absolute equality—otherwise we could not have referred to that standard the equals derived from the senses. For to that they all aspire, and of that they all fall short.
No other conclusion can be drawn from what was said before.
And did we not see and hear and make use of our other senses as soon as we were born?
Certainly.
Then we must have acquired the knowledge of equality at some earlier time?
Yes.
That is to say, before we were born, I suppose?
True.

And if we acquired this knowledge before we were born, and were born already possessing it, then we knew before birth and at the very moment of birth not only the equal or the greater or the less, but all other Ideas as well. For we are not speaking only of equality, but of beauty, goodness, justice, holiness, and everything we mark with the name of essence in the dialectical process, both when we ask and when we answer questions. Of all this we can certainly affirm that we acquired the knowledge before birth?
We can.

But if, after acquiring it, we have not forgotten what we learned in each case, then we must always have come into life already knowing, and must always continue to know as long as life lasts—for knowing is acquiring and retaining knowledge and not forgetting. Isn't forgetting, Simmias, just the losing of knowledge?
Quite true, Socrates.

But if the knowledge we acquired before birth was lost by us at birth, and if afterwards, by use of the senses, we recovered what we previously knew, then won't the process we call learning be a recovering of knowledge that is natural to us—and mightn't this rightly be called recollection?
Very true.

So much is clear: when we perceive something by sight, hearing, or another sense, from that perception we can get a notion of some other thing, like or unlike, which is associated with it but has been forgotten. So, as I was saying, one of two alternatives follows: either we had this knowledge at birth and continued to know throughout life; or else those said to learn, after birth, are only remembering, and learning is simply recollection.
Yes, that is quite true, Socrates.
And which alternative, Simmias, do you prefer? Did we have the knowledge at birth, or do we recollect the things we knew prior to birth?
I cannot decide at the moment.
At any rate you can decide this: will someone who has knowledge be able to give an account of it, or not? What do you say?
Certainly, he will.
But do you think every man is able to give an account of the matters we are discussing?
I wish they could, Socrates, but I rather fear that tomorrow, at this time, there will no longer be anyone alive able to give such an account as ought to be given.
Then you are not of the opinion, Simmias, that all men know these things?
Certainly not.
They are in the process of recollecting what they learned before?
Certainly.
But when did our souls acquire this knowledge?—not since we were born as men?
Certainly not.
And therefore, at some earlier time?
Yes.
Then, Simmias, our souls must also have existed without bodies before they took human form, and must have had intelligence.
Unless, Socrates, you suppose these notions are given to us at the very moment of birth—for that is the only time that remains.
Yes, my friend, but if so, when do we lose them? We agreed they are not in us when we are born. Do we lose them at the moment of receiving them, or if not then, at what other time?
No, Socrates—I see that I was unconsciously talking nonsense.

Then may we not say this, Simmias: if, as we keep repeating, there is an absolute beauty, and goodness, and an absolute essence of all things; and if we refer all our sensations to this essence—which now proves to have existed in our former state—and compare them with it, finding these Ideas to be pre-existent and our inborn possession—then our souls must have had a prior existence; but if not, there would be no force in the argument? The proof that these Ideas must have existed before we were born is the same as the proof that our souls existed before we were born; and if not the Ideas, then not the souls.

Yes, Socrates; I am convinced that there is exactly the same necessity for the one as for the other, and the argument retreats safely to the position that the existence of the soul before birth cannot be separated from the existence of the essence you speak of. For to my mind nothing is more evident than that beauty, goodness, and the other notions you were just now mentioning have a most real and absolute existence; and I am satisfied with the proof.
Well, but is Cebes equally satisfied? For I must convince him too.

I think, Simmias said, that Cebes is satisfied—although he is the most incredulous of mortals, I believe he is sufficiently convinced of the existence of the soul before birth. But that the soul will continue to exist after death is not yet proven even to my own satisfaction. I cannot shake the feeling of the many to which Cebes was referring—the feeling that when a man dies the soul may be dispersed, and that this may be the end of her. For granted that she may have been born elsewhere, framed out of other elements, and was in existence before entering the human body, why, after she has entered in and then gone out again, may she not herself be destroyed and come to an end?

Very true, Simmias, said Cebes; about half of what is required has been proven—namely, that our souls existed before we were born. That the soul will exist after death as well as before birth is the other half, still needing proof; when that is given, the demonstration will be complete.

But that proof, Simmias and Cebes, has already been given, said Socrates, if you put the two arguments together—I mean this one and the earlier one, in which we admitted that everything living is born from the dead. For if the soul exists before birth, and in coming to life and being born can only be born from death and dying, must she not also continue to exist after death, since she has to be born again?—Surely the proof you want has already been supplied. Still, I suspect that you and Simmias would be glad to press the argument further. Like children, you are haunted by the fear that when the soul leaves the body the wind may really blow her away and scatter her—especially if a man happens to die in a great storm and not when the sky is calm.

Cebes answered with a smile: Then, Socrates, you must argue us out of our fears—though strictly speaking they are not our fears, but there is a child within us to whom death is a kind of hobgoblin; him too we must persuade not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark.
Socrates said: Let the voice of the charmer be applied daily until you have charmed the fear away.
And where shall we find a good charmer of our fears, Socrates, when you are gone?

Hellas, he replied, is a large place, Cebes, and has many good men, and there are no few barbarian peoples either: seek such a charmer among them all, far and wide, sparing neither effort nor money; for there is no better way to spend your money. And you must search among yourselves too, for you will not find others more able to make the search.
The search, replied Cebes, shall certainly be made. And now, if you please, let us return to the point in the argument at which we digressed.
By all means, replied Socrates; what else should I please?
Very good.

Must we not ask ourselves, said Socrates, what sort of thing it is that we imagine to be liable to be scattered, and about which we fear? And what sort of thing it is about which we have no fear? And then we can go on to inquire whether that which suffers dispersion is of the nature of soul or not—our hopes and fears about our own souls will turn on the answers to these questions.
Very true, he said.

Now the compound or composite may be supposed naturally capable of being dissolved, just as it was of being compounded; but the uncompounded—and only the uncompounded—must be, if anything is, indissoluble.
Yes; I should imagine so, said Cebes.
And the uncompounded may be assumed to be the same and unchanging, whereas the compound is always changing and never the same.
I agree, he said.

Then let us return to the earlier discussion. That Idea or essence which in the dialectical process we define as essence or true existence—whether the essence of equality, of beauty, or of anything else—are these essences ever liable to some degree of change? Or is each of them always what it is, having the same simple self-existent and unchanging form, admitting no variation at all, in any way, or at any time?
They must always be the same, Socrates, replied Cebes.

And what would you say of the many beautiful things—whether men or horses or garments or anything else called by the same names and spoken of as equal or beautiful? Are they all unchanging and always the same, or quite the reverse? Might they not rather be described as almost always changing and hardly ever the same, either with themselves or with one another?
The latter, replied Cebes; they are always in a state of change.
And these you can touch and see and perceive with the senses, but the unchanging things you can only perceive with the mind—they are invisible and are not seen?
That is very true, he said.
Well then, Socrates added, let us suppose there are two sorts of existences—one seen, the other unseen.
Let us suppose them.
The seen is the changing, and the unseen is the unchanging?
That may also be supposed.
And further, is not one part of us body, and another part soul?
To be sure.
And to which class is the body more alike and akin?
Clearly to the seen—no one can doubt that.
And is the soul seen, or not seen?
Not by man, Socrates.
And what we mean by 'seen' and 'not seen' is what is or is not visible to the eye of man?
Yes, to the eye of man.
And is the soul seen, or not seen?
Not seen.
Unseen, then?
Yes.
Then the soul is more like the unseen, and the body more like the seen?
That follows necessarily, Socrates.

And weren't we saying long ago that the soul, when using the body as an instrument of perception—that is, when using the sense of sight or hearing or some other sense (for perceiving through the body means perceiving through the senses)—weren't we saying that the soul is then dragged by the body into the region of the changeable, and wanders and is confused? The world spins round her, and she is like a drunkard whenever she touches change?
Very true.

But when she returns into herself and reflects, then she passes into the other world—the region of purity, eternity, immortality, and unchangeableness, which are her kindred; and with them she forever dwells whenever she is by herself and is not hindered. Then she ceases from her wandering, and being in communion with the unchanging, is herself unchanging. And this state of the soul is called wisdom?
That is well and truly said, Socrates, he replied.
And to which class is the soul more nearly alike and akin, as far as may be inferred from this argument and from the one before?
I think, Socrates, that in the opinion of anyone who follows the argument, the soul will be infinitely more like the unchangeable—even the most stupid person would not deny that.
And the body is more like the changing?
Yes.

Consider the matter once more in another light. When the soul and the body are united, nature orders the soul to rule and govern, and the body to obey and serve. Now which of these two functions is akin to the divine, and which to the mortal? Doesn't the divine appear to you to be that which naturally orders and rules, and the mortal to be that which is subject and servant?
True.
And which does the soul resemble?
The soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal—there can be no doubt of that, Socrates.

Then reflect, Cebes: of all that has been said, is this not the conclusion?—that the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal, and intellectual, and uniform, and indissoluble, and unchangeable; and that the body is in the very likeness of the human, and mortal, and unintellectual, and multiform, and dissoluble, and changeable. Can this, my dear Cebes, be denied?
It cannot.
But if so, then is not the body liable to speedy dissolution? And is not the soul almost or altogether indissoluble?
Certainly.

Observe further: after a man is dead, the body—the visible part of him, which lies in the visible world and is called a corpse, and would naturally be dissolved and decomposed and scattered—does not dissolve or decompose at once, but may remain for some time, even a long time, if the constitution was sound at the time of death and the season of the year is favorable. For the body, when shrunk and embalmed as they do in Egypt, may remain almost whole for countless ages; and even in decay, some parts such as the bones and ligaments are practically indestructible. Do you agree?
Yes.

And is it likely that the soul, which is invisible, in passing to the place of the true Hades—which, like her, is invisible, and pure, and noble, and on her way to the good and wise God (where, if God wills, my soul too is soon to go)—is it likely, I say, that the soul, if this be her nature and origin, will be blown away and destroyed the moment she leaves the body, as the many say? That can never be, my dear Simmias and Cebes. The truth rather is this: the soul which is pure at departing and drags no bodily taint after her, having never willingly during life had anything to do with the body—which she has always been avoiding, gathering herself into herself, and making such abstraction her constant practice—which means that she has been a true disciple of philosophy, and has therefore in fact always been practicing how to die. For is not philosophy the practice of death?—
Certainly—

That soul, I say, herself invisible, departs to the invisible world—to the divine, the immortal, the rational. On arriving there, she is secure of bliss and is released from the error and folly of men, from their fears and wild passions and all other human evils, and forever dwells, as they say of the initiated, in the company of the gods. Is this not true, Cebes?
Yes, said Cebes, beyond a doubt.

But the soul that has been polluted, and is impure at the time of her departure, and has been the companion and servant of the body always, and is in love with it and fascinated by it and by the body's desires and pleasures, until she comes to believe that the truth exists only in bodily form—something a man can touch and see and taste and use for his lusts—such a soul, accustomed to hate and fear and avoid the intellectual principle, which to the bodily eye is dark and invisible and can be attained only by philosophy—do you suppose that such a soul will depart pure and unalloyed?
Impossible, he replied.
She is held fast by the corporeal, which the continual association and constant care of the body have wrought into her nature.
Very true.

And this corporeal element, my friend, is heavy and weighty and earthy, and is that element of sight by which a soul is depressed and dragged down again into the visible world, because she is afraid of the invisible and of the world below—prowling about tombs and graves, near which, as they tell us, are seen certain ghostly apparitions of souls that have not departed pure, but are clogged with sight and therefore visible.
(Compare Milton, Comus:—

'But when lust, By unchaste looks, loose gestures, and foul talk, But most by lewd and lavish act of sin, Lets in defilement to the inward parts, The soul grows clotted by contagion, Imbodies, and imbrutes, till she quite lose, The divine property of her first being. Such are those thick and gloomy shadows damp Oft seen in charnel vaults and sepulchres, Lingering, and sitting by a new made grave, As loath to leave the body that it lov'd, And linked itself by carnal sensuality To a degenerate and degraded state.')
That is very likely, Socrates.

Yes, that is very likely, Cebes; and these must be the souls, not of the good, but of the wicked, which are compelled to wander about such places in payment of the penalty for their former evil way of life. And they continue to wander until, through the craving after the corporeal that never leaves them, they are at last imprisoned in another body. And they may be supposed to find their prisons in the same natures they had in their former lives.
What natures do you mean, Socrates?
I mean that men who have followed gluttony, wantonness, and drunkenness, and have never troubled to avoid them, would pass into asses and animals of that sort. What do you think?
I think that opinion to be exceedingly probable.
And those who have chosen the portion of injustice, tyranny, and violence will pass into wolves, or into hawks and kites—where else could we suppose them to go?
Yes, said Cebes; with such natures, beyond question.
And there is no difficulty, he said, in assigning to all of them places answering to their several natures and dispositions?
There is not, he said.

Some are happier than others; and the happiest, both in themselves and in the place they go, are those who have practiced the civil and social virtues called temperance and justice, which are acquired by habit and attention without philosophy and intelligence.
Why are they the happiest?

Because they may be expected to pass into some gentle and social kind which is like their own, such as bees or wasps or ants, or back again into the form of man; and just and moderate men may be supposed to spring from them.
Very likely.

No one who has not studied philosophy, and is not entirely pure at the time of his departure, is allowed to enter the company of the Gods—only the lover of knowledge is. And this is the reason, Simmias and Cebes, why the true devotees of philosophy abstain from all fleshly lusts, and hold out against them and refuse to give themselves up to them—not because they fear poverty or the ruin of their families, like the lovers of money and the world in general; nor like the lovers of power and honor, because they dread the dishonor and disgrace of evil deeds.
No, Socrates, that would not suit them, said Cebes.

No indeed, he replied; and therefore those who have any care of their own souls, and do not merely live molding and fashioning the body, say farewell to all this. They will not walk in the ways of the blind; and when philosophy offers them purification and release from evil, they feel they ought not to resist her influence, and wherever she leads they turn and follow.
What do you mean, Socrates?

I will tell you, he said. The lovers of knowledge are conscious that the soul was simply fastened and glued to the body—that until philosophy received her, she could view real existence only through the bars of a prison, not in and through herself; that she was wallowing in the mire of every kind of ignorance, and that through lust she had become the principal accomplice in her own captivity. This was her original state; and then, as I was saying, and as the lovers of knowledge are well aware, philosophy, seeing how dreadful her confinement was—of which she herself was the cause—received her and gently comforted her, and sought to release her, pointing out that the eye and the ear and the other senses are full of deception, and persuading her to withdraw from them, and to abstain from all but their necessary use, and to be gathered up and collected into herself, bidding her trust in herself and in her own pure apprehension of pure existence, and to mistrust whatever comes to her through other channels and is subject to variation; for such things are visible and tangible, but what she sees in her own nature is intelligible and invisible.

And the soul of the true philosopher thinks she ought not to resist this deliverance, and therefore abstains from pleasures and desires and pains and fears, as far as she is able—reflecting that when a man has great joys or sorrows or fears or desires, he suffers from them not merely the sort of evil one might expect, such as the loss of health or property that he has sacrificed to his lusts, but an evil far greater, the greatest and worst of all evils, and one that he never even thinks about.
What is it, Socrates? said Cebes.

The evil is this: when the feeling of pleasure or pain is most intense, every soul of man imagines that the objects of this intense feeling are then plainest and truest; but this is not so—they are really the things of sight.
Very true.
And is not this the state in which the soul is most enthralled by the body?
How so?

Why, because each pleasure and pain is a kind of nail that nails and rivets the soul to the body, until she becomes like the body and believes whatever the body affirms to be true. By agreeing with the body and sharing the same delights, she is forced to share the same habits and haunts, and is not likely ever to be pure at her departure to the world below, but is always infected by the body. And so she sinks into another body and germinates and grows there, and has therefore no share in the communion of the divine and pure and simple.
Most true, Socrates, answered Cebes.
And this, Cebes, is the reason why the true lovers of knowledge are temperate and brave; and not for the reason the world gives.
Certainly not.

Certainly not! The soul of a philosopher will reason in quite another way. She will not ask philosophy to release her so that when released she may deliver herself up again to the thraldom of pleasures and pains, doing a work only to undo it again, weaving instead of unweaving her Penelope's web. Rather, she will calm passion, and follow reason, and dwell in the contemplation of her, beholding the true and divine (which is no matter of opinion), and from that drawing her nourishment. Thus she seeks to live while she lives, and after death she hopes to go to her own kindred and to that which is like her, and to be freed from human ills. Never fear, Simmias and Cebes, that a soul which has been thus nurtured and has pursued these things will at her departure from the body be scattered and blown away by the winds and be nowhere and nothing.

When Socrates had finished speaking, there was silence for a considerable time. He himself seemed to be meditating, as most of us were, on what had been said; only Cebes and Simmias spoke a few words to one another. And Socrates, observing them, asked what they thought of the argument, and whether there was anything still wanting. For, said he, there are many points still open to suspicion and attack, if one were inclined to sift the matter thoroughly. If you are considering some other matter, I say no more; but if you are still in doubt, do not hesitate to say exactly what you think, and let us hear anything better you can suggest; and if you think I can be of any use, allow me to help you.

Simmias said: I must confess, Socrates, that doubts did arise in our minds, and each of us was urging and inciting the other to put the question we wanted answered, yet neither of us liked to ask, fearing that our importunity might be troublesome to you at such a time.

Socrates replied with a smile: O Simmias, what are you saying? I am hardly likely to persuade other men that I do not regard my present situation as a misfortune, if I cannot even persuade you that I am no worse off now than at any other time in my life. Will you not allow that I have as much of the spirit of prophecy in me as the swans? For when they perceive that they must die, having sung all their life long, they then sing more lustily than ever, rejoicing in the thought that they are about to depart to the god whose ministers they are. But men, because they are themselves afraid of death, slanderously say that the swans sing a lament at the last—not considering that no bird sings when cold or hungry or in pain, not even the nightingale, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, who are indeed said to tune a lay of sorrow, though I do not believe this to be true of them any more than of the swans. Rather, because they are sacred to Apollo, they have the gift of prophecy and foresee the good things of another world, which is why they sing and rejoice on that day more than they ever did before. And I too, believing myself to be the consecrated servant of the same God, and a fellow-servant of the swans, and thinking that I have received from my master gifts of prophecy not inferior to theirs, would not go out of life any less cheerfully than the swans.
Never mind that, then, if this is your only objection—but speak, and ask anything you like, while the eleven magistrates of Athens allow.

Very good, Socrates, said Simmias; then I will tell you my difficulty, and Cebes will tell you his. I feel myself (and I dare say you have the same feeling) how hard, or rather how impossible, it is to attain any certainty about questions such as these in the present life. And yet I should think him a coward who did not test what is said about them to the uttermost, or whose heart failed him before he had examined them on every side. He ought to persevere until he has achieved one of two things: either he should discover, or be taught, the truth about them; or, if that is impossible, he should take the best and most irrefragable of human theories, and let this be the raft upon which he sails through life—not without risk, as I admit, if he cannot find some word of God to carry him more surely and safely. And now, as you bid me, I will venture to question you, so that I shall not afterwards reproach myself with not having said at the time what I think. For when I consider the matter, either alone or with Cebes, the argument does certainly appear to me, Socrates, to be not sufficient.
Socrates answered: I dare say, my friend, that you may be right; but I should like to know in what respect the argument is insufficient.

chapters.title: The Objections
paragraphs: 'Here's my difficulty,' replied Simmias. 'Someone could use the same argument about a lyre and its harmony. They could say: harmony is invisible, incorporeal, perfectly beautiful, and divine — existing in a well-tuned lyre. But the lyre and its strings are material, composite, earthy, and mortal. Now if someone breaks the lyre or cuts the strings, your style of reasoning would lead us to say the harmony must survive — that surely the mortal lyre and broken strings still exist, so the harmony, being divine and immortal, can't have perished first. The harmony must still be somewhere, and the wood and strings will decay before anything happens to it. I imagine, Socrates, that you've had the same thought I have: that this is roughly our conception of the soul. When the body is strung together and held in balance by hot and cold, wet and dry, the soul is the harmony — the proper blending of these elements. If that's true, then whenever the body's strings are loosened or overstrained by disease or other injury, the soul — however divine — must immediately perish, just as other harmonies in music perish. The body's remains may last a long time before they're burned or decay. But the soul would be the first to be destroyed in what we call death.'
'And if someone insists that the soul, being a harmony of the body's elements, is the first to perish in death — how shall we answer him?'

Socrates looked intently at us with his penetrating eyes, smiled, and said: 'Simmias raises a fair point. If any of you has a better answer than I do, speak up — his attack has real force. But before we respond to him, I think we should hear what Cebes has to say as well, so we can take time to think. After hearing both, we can either agree with them if they're right, or defend our position if not. So tell me, Cebes — what was troubling you?'

chapters.title: The Final Argument
paragraphs: 'I'll tell you,' said Cebes. 'The argument seems to me to be exactly where it was, open to the same objections. I'm ready to admit that the soul's existence before entering the body has been ingeniously — even convincingly — proven. But that the soul exists after death remains, in my judgment, unproven. My objection isn't the same as Simmias's — I don't deny that the soul is stronger and more lasting than the body. I think the soul far excels the body in every such respect. "Well then," the argument says, "why aren't you convinced? If the weaker part survives death, surely the more lasting part must too?" But consider this analogy — like Simmias, I'll use a figure of speech. Imagine an old weaver dies. Someone says: "He's not dead — he must be alive. Look, the coat he wove and wore is still intact." And when a doubter asks whether a man or his coat is more durable, and is told a man lasts far longer, the fool thinks he's proven the man must still exist because the less durable coat survives.'

'But that, Simmias, is a mistake — anyone can see it's nonsense. The weaver wove and wore out many coats during his life. He outlasted them all except the last. But a man isn't proved weaker than a coat just because the last one survives him. The same applies to soul and body: one might fairly say the soul is lasting while the body is comparatively weak and short-lived. Every soul wears out many bodies, especially over a long life — the body is always changing and being renewed while we live, and the soul keeps weaving new garments. But when the soul finally perishes, she must be wearing her last body. That body will survive her briefly, then quickly show its natural weakness and decompose. So I'd rather not rely on the argument from superior strength to prove the soul survives death.'

'Even if we grant more than you claim — that the soul existed before birth, and that some souls continue to exist after death, being born and dying repeatedly, possessing natural strength enough to endure many lifetimes — even so, the soul might eventually wear out in these successive births and finally perish in one of its deaths. And this particular death might be unknown to any of us, since no one has experienced it. If so, then anyone who faces death confidently is a fool — unless they can prove the soul is entirely immortal and imperishable. Without that proof, every dying person has reason to fear that this death may be the one in which the soul is destroyed.'

All of us, as we later told each other, felt deeply troubled by what they said. We'd been so firmly convinced, and now our faith was shaken — throwing doubt not just on the previous argument but on anything we might ever be told. Perhaps we were incapable of judging, or perhaps the whole subject was beyond certainty.

ECHECRATES: I feel exactly the same, Phaedo — by heaven I do! As I listen to you, I find myself thinking: what argument can I trust anymore? Socrates' reasoning had seemed so convincing, and now it's fallen into doubt. The theory that the soul is a harmony has always had a strong grip on me, and hearing it raised again reminded me that I need a whole new argument to be convinced that the soul survives death. Tell me, I beg you — how did Socrates respond? Did he seem as shaken as the rest of you, or did he calmly meet the attack? Was his answer strong or weak? Tell me everything you can.

PHAEDO: I've often marveled at Socrates, Echecrates, but never more than that day. That he had an answer wasn't surprising — what amazed me was the gentle, approving way he received the young men's objections, his quick perception of the wound they'd inflicted on the argument, and the readiness with which he healed it. He was like a general rallying his defeated army, urging them to regroup and return to the field.
ECHECRATES: What happened next?

PHAEDO: You'll hear — I was sitting close to him on his right, on a low stool, while he was on a much higher couch. He stroked my head and pressed the hair on my neck — he had a habit of playing with my hair. Then he said: 'Tomorrow, Phaedo, I suppose these beautiful locks of yours will be cut off.'
'Yes, Socrates, I suppose they will,' I replied.
'Not if you take my advice.'
'What should I do with them?' I asked.

'Today,' he replied, 'not tomorrow — if this argument dies and we can't bring it back to life — you and I will both shave our heads. If I were you, and the argument slipped away, I'd swear like the Argives never to grow my hair back until I'd renewed the fight and defeated Simmias and Cebes.'
'But even Heracles, they say, was no match for two,' I said.
'Then call me in as your Iolaus,' he said, 'before the sun goes down.'
'I summon you,' I replied, 'not as Heracles summoning Iolaus, but as Iolaus summoning Heracles.'
'It amounts to the same thing,' he said. 'But first, let's be careful to avoid a danger.'
'What danger?' I asked.

'The danger of becoming misologists — haters of arguments — just as some people become misanthropes, haters of humanity. Both spring from the same cause: ignorance. Misanthropy arises from excessive, naive trust: you trust someone completely, believing them to be honest and true, and then discover they're false. Then another, and another. When this happens repeatedly — especially with those you considered your closest friends — you end up hating everyone and believing that no person has any good in them. You've noticed this, haven't you?'
'I have.'
'Isn't it disgraceful? Clearly such a person has no experience of human nature. Experience teaches the truth: very good and very bad people are both rare — most people are somewhere in between.'
'What do you mean?' I said.

'Think of extremes — very large or very small, very fast or slow, very beautiful or ugly, very light or dark. In every case, the extremes are rare while the middle is common. Whether you're talking about people, dogs, or anything else. Haven't you noticed?'
'Yes, I have.'
'And if there were a competition in evil, wouldn't the truly worst be very few?'
'Very likely,' I said.

'Very likely indeed,' he replied. 'Though in this respect arguments are unlike people — you led me into saying more than I intended. The real comparison is this: when a simple person who lacks skill in reasoning believes an argument is true, and then discovers — or thinks — it's false, and then the same happens again and again, they lose all faith. The greatest debaters end up thinking they're the wisest people alive, because they alone have discovered that nothing in the world is sound or stable — that everything ebbs and flows like the currents in the Euripus.'
'That's very true,' I said.

'Yes, Phaedo — and how tragic, if there really is truth and certainty and knowledge to be found, that someone should stumble upon an argument that first seemed true and then false, and instead of blaming their own lack of skill, end up hating arguments altogether, losing truth and the knowledge of reality for the rest of their lives.'
'Yes indeed — that's very tragic,' I said.

'So first of all,' he said, 'let's be careful not to admit into our souls the idea that arguments are fundamentally unsound. Rather, let's say that we ourselves aren't yet sound, and that we must work hard to become so — you and everyone else, for the sake of your whole future lives, and I for the sake of my death. Right now, I confess, I don't have the temperament of a philosopher — I'm more like a partisan. A partisan in a debate cares nothing about truth; he only wants to persuade his audience. The difference between him and me right now is simply this: he wants to convince his listeners that what he says is true, while I'm trying to convince myself. Convincing you is secondary. And see what I gain: if what I say is true, I do well to believe it. If there's nothing after death, at least I won't distress my friends with lamentations during this little time that remains, and my ignorance will die with me. So no harm is done. This is my frame of mind, Simmias and Cebes, as I approach the argument.'

'And I ask you to think about truth, not about Socrates. If I seem to speak truly, agree with me. If not, resist me with all your strength — don't let me deceive you along with myself in my enthusiasm, like a bee that leaves its sting behind and dies.'

'Now let's proceed,' he said. 'First, let me be sure I understand your objections. Simmias, if I recall correctly, fears that the soul — though nobler and more divine than the body, being a kind of harmony — might perish first. Cebes grants that the soul is more lasting than the body, but says no one can know whether, after wearing out many bodies, the soul might not finally perish herself — and that this would be the true death, not of the body but of the soul, since the body is always in a state of decay. Are these your concerns?'
They both agreed this was accurate.
'Now — did you reject the whole preceding argument, or only part of it?'
'Only part,' they replied.
'And what did you think of the part where we said knowledge is recollection — implying that the soul must have existed somewhere else before being enclosed in the body?'
Cebes said he'd been wonderfully impressed by that argument and remained completely convinced. Simmias agreed — he could hardly imagine ever thinking differently.

'But you'll have to think differently, my Theban friend,' rejoined Socrates, 'if you still hold that the soul is a harmony made from the body's elements. You'll never allow yourself to say that a harmony existed before the parts that compose it.'
'Never, Socrates.'

'But don't you see that's exactly what you imply when you say the soul existed before taking human form, while being made of elements that didn't yet exist? A harmony isn't like the soul as you describe it — the lyre, the strings, and the sounds must exist first, in a state of discord, and then harmony comes into being last and perishes first. How can your theory of the soul agree with the recollection argument?'
'It can't,' replied Simmias.
'And yet,' said Socrates, 'there ought to be harmony in a discourse whose theme is harmony.'
'There ought,' replied Simmias.
'But your two propositions are dissonant: that knowledge is recollection, and that the soul is a harmony. Which will you keep?'

'I have far stronger faith in the recollection argument, which has been properly demonstrated, than in the harmony theory, which rests only on plausible probability and is believed by the many. I know all too well that arguments from probability are unreliable — in geometry and everything else. But the recollection doctrine was proven on solid grounds: the soul must have existed before the body because she possesses the essence that implies existence. Having accepted this conclusion, I must reject the idea that the soul is a harmony.'
'Let me put it another way, Simmias: Can a harmony or any compound exist in a state other than the state of its component parts?'
'Certainly not.'
'Or do or suffer anything other than what they do or suffer?'
He agreed.
'Then a harmony doesn't lead its parts — it follows them?'
He agreed.
'A harmony can have no motion, sound, or quality that opposes its parts?'
'Impossible,' he replied.
'Doesn't every harmony depend on how its elements are combined?'
'I don't understand,' he said.
'I mean that a harmony can be more or less complete — more fully harmonized to whatever degree is possible, or less fully harmonized.'
'True.'
'But does the soul admit of degrees? Is one soul even slightly more or less a soul than another?'
'Not in the least.'
'Yet surely one soul is said to have intelligence and virtue — to be good — while another has folly and vice — to be evil? And this is said truly?'
'Yes, truly.'
'But what would those who say the soul is a harmony make of virtue and vice? Would they say there's another harmony within the harmonious soul, and discord within the vicious one?'
'I can't say,' replied Simmias, 'but I suppose something like that would be claimed.'
'But we've already agreed that no soul is more a soul than another — which means no harmony is more or less a harmony?'
'Quite true.'
'And what is not more or less a harmony is not more or less harmonized?'
'True.'
'And what is not more or less harmonized can't have more or less harmony — only equal harmony?'
'Yes, equal harmony.'
'So one soul, being no more or less a soul than another, is not more or less harmonized?'
'Exactly.'
'And therefore has neither more nor less of discord or harmony?'
'She has not.'
'And having no more or less harmony or discord, one soul has no more vice or virtue than another — if vice is discord and virtue is harmony?'
'Not at all more.'
'Or more correctly, Simmias: if the soul is a harmony, she can never have any vice at all — because a perfect harmony has no share in disharmony.'
'No.'
'And a soul that is absolutely a soul has no vice?'
'How could she, if the previous argument holds?'
'Then if all souls are equally souls by nature, all souls of all living creatures would be equally good?'
'I agree, Socrates,' he said.
'And can all this be true? Are these the consequences of saying the soul is a harmony?'
'It can't be true.'
'One more thing: what rules the human being other than the soul — especially the wise soul? Do you know of any such ruler?'
'No, I don't.'

'Does the soul agree with the body's impulses, or oppose them? When the body is hot and thirsty, doesn't the soul urge us not to drink? When hungry, not to eat? And these are just examples among thousands of the soul opposing the body.'
'Very true.'
'But we agreed that the soul — if she's a harmony — can never sound a note at variance with the tensions and vibrations of the strings she's composed from. She can only follow, never lead?'
'Yes, that must be so,' he replied.

'Yet now we discover the soul doing the exact opposite — leading the elements she's supposedly composed of, opposing and controlling them throughout life. Sometimes harshly, through the pains of medicine and exercise. Sometimes gently — threatening, warning, admonishing desires and passions and fears, as though speaking to something other than herself. As Homer writes of Odysseus:'
'"He struck his chest and spoke to his own heart: Endure, my heart — you have endured far worse."'

'Do you think Homer wrote this imagining the soul is a harmony that can be led by bodily feelings? Or rather that the soul's nature is to lead and master them — being something far more divine than any harmony?'
'Definitely the latter, Socrates.'
'Then, my friend, we can never be right in calling the soul a harmony — we'd contradict the divine Homer, and contradict ourselves.'
'True,' he said.
'So much,' said Socrates, 'for Harmonia, your Theban goddess, who has graciously yielded to us. But what about her husband Cadmus, Cebes? How shall I make peace with him?'

'I'm sure you'll find a way,' said Cebes. 'Your argument against Harmonia surprised me completely — I thought Simmias' objection was unanswerable, but it couldn't survive the first blow of yours. Perhaps Cadmus will share the same fate.'

'Don't tempt fate,' said Socrates. 'Some evil eye might put the argument to flight. But that's in the hands of the gods. Let me now, Homeric fashion, test the mettle of your argument. Here's the core of it: you want proof that the soul is imperishable and immortal, and you think the philosopher who faces death confidently is foolish unless he can prove he'll fare better than someone who lived differently. You say that demonstrating the soul's strength, divinity, and prior existence doesn't prove immortality. Even if the soul is long-lived and experienced, her entrance into the human body might be the beginning of her destruction — a kind of disease that eventually, after life's toils, ends in what we call death. And whether the soul enters the body once or many times makes no difference to the fear: any rational person must be afraid unless they can prove the soul is altogether immortal.'
'That's my position, or something close to it,' said Cebes. 'I repeat it so nothing escapes us, and so you can add or subtract anything.'
'As far as I can see,' said Cebes, 'I have nothing to add or subtract. That's what I mean.'

Socrates paused and seemed absorbed in thought. At length he said: 'You're raising a tremendous question, Cebes — it involves the entire nature of generation and corruption. If you like, I'll tell you about my own experience with this subject. If anything I say might help solve your difficulty, you're welcome to use it.'
'I'd very much like to hear,' said Cebes.

'Then I'll tell you. When I was young, Cebes, I had an enormous desire to understand what they call the investigation of nature — to know the causes of things, why things exist, why they come into being and pass away.
