I was always asking myself: Is animal growth the result of some chemical reaction, as some claim? Is blood the element we think with — or air, or fire? Or is it none of these — perhaps the brain produces perception of sight, hearing, and smell, and from these come memory and opinion, and from stable memory and opinion comes knowledge? Then I went on to investigate how these things decay, and then the phenomena of heaven and earth. In the end I concluded I was utterly incapable of this kind of inquiry — as I'll prove to you.'

'I was so captivated by these questions that things I'd previously understood perfectly well became obscure. I forgot what had seemed self-evident: for example, that humans grow because of eating and drinking — when food is digested, flesh is added to flesh, bone to bone, and by accumulation the small becomes large. That seemed obvious, didn't it?'
'Yes,' said Cebes, 'I think so.'

'And I used to think I understood why one person is taller than another — by a head, for instance — or why ten is more than eight by two, or why two cubits is more than one cubit because it's double.'
'And what do you think now?' said Cebes.

'I'm very far from imagining I understand the cause of any of these things! I can't even understand how, when one is added to one, either the one that's added or the one it's added to becomes two — or how both together become two by being brought together. I can't understand how mere juxtaposition makes two. Nor can I understand how dividing one thing in two is the way to make two — since that's the opposite cause. I'm no longer satisfied that I understand why anything comes into being, exists, or is destroyed. I have only a confused notion of a new method, and can't accept the old one at all.'

'Then I heard someone reading from a book by Anaxagoras, saying that Mind is the arranger and cause of all things. I was delighted — this seemed wonderful. If Mind arranges everything, I thought, it must arrange everything for the best. To find the cause of anything, you just need to find what's best for it. I imagined Anaxagoras would explain why the earth is flat or round, and then show that this shape was best. If the earth is at the center, he'd explain why that position is best. I was going to ask him about the sun, moon, and stars too — their speeds, orbits, and interactions — and how all their arrangements are for the best.'

'I couldn't imagine that when he spoke of Mind as the cause, he'd give any other explanation except that this arrangement was best. I thought he'd explain the cause of each thing individually and the cause of everything collectively by showing what was best. I wouldn't have sold these hopes for any amount of money. I seized his books and read them as fast as I could.'

'What expectations I had — and how bitterly I was disappointed! As I read on, I found my philosopher abandoning Mind and having nothing to do with order or purpose, but resorting to air, ether, water, and other absurdities.'

'It was as if someone began by saying that Mind is the cause of everything Socrates does, but then, trying to explain my specific actions, said: Socrates sits here because his body is made of bones and muscles — the bones are hard and have joints, the muscles are elastic and wrap around the bones with flesh and skin. Because the bones move at their joints through the contraction and relaxation of muscles, Socrates can bend his limbs — and that's why he's sitting here in this curved position. And he'd give similar explanations for my talking to you — sound, air, hearing, and ten thousand other causes — while forgetting to mention the real cause: that the Athenians decided to condemn me, and I decided it was better and more right to stay here and accept my sentence. Otherwise these bones and muscles of mine would have taken themselves off to Megara or Boeotia long ago — by the dog they would — if I'd been moved only by what seemed best for my body rather than choosing the nobler course of accepting whatever punishment the state imposes. There's a strange confusion of causes and conditions in all this.'

'You might say that without bones and muscles I couldn't carry out my decisions — and that would be true. But to say I act the way I do because of bones and muscles, rather than from my choice of what is best — that's lazy and careless reasoning. It confuses the cause with the condition. One person makes a vortex the cause of everything and says the heavens hold the earth in place. Another says the earth rests on air like a broad trough. But the power that arranges things as they are because it's best never enters their minds. Instead of recognizing the superiority of the good, they expect to find some Atlas stronger and more everlasting than goodness itself. They think nothing of the binding, constraining power of the good. I would gladly have learned about this power from anyone who could teach me. But since I failed to discover it myself, or to learn it from anyone else, let me show you what I found to be the second-best method of inquiring into causes.'
'I'd very much like to hear,' he replied.

'After I'd failed in contemplating things directly, I realized I had to be careful not to blind my soul's eye — the way people damage their physical eyes by looking at the sun during an eclipse without looking at a reflection in water instead. So I decided I'd better turn to the world of thought and seek truth there. My analogy isn't perfect — I certainly don't admit that someone who examines things through thought sees them only "through a glass darkly" compared to someone who observes them directly. But this was my method: I'd start with whatever principle I judged strongest, and then accept as true whatever agreed with it — regarding causes or anything else — and reject as false whatever didn't. But let me explain more clearly, because I don't think you follow me yet.'
'No, not very well,' replied Cebes.

'There's nothing new in what I'm about to say — it's what I've always been saying. I want to show you the nature of the cause that has occupied my mind. I'll return to those familiar ideas that are on everyone's lips: I start by assuming that there is an absolute beauty, an absolute goodness, an absolute greatness, and so on. Grant me this, and I hope to show you the nature of the cause and prove the soul's immortality.'
'You may proceed,' said Cebes. 'I grant you this.'

'Then tell me if you agree with the next step: I believe that if anything is beautiful besides absolute beauty, it can be beautiful only insofar as it participates in absolute beauty. The same applies to everything. Do you accept this kind of causation?'
'Yes, I do,' he said.

'Then I know nothing of those other clever causes people propose — and can understand nothing of them. If someone tells me that a thing is beautiful because of its color, or shape, or anything else of that sort — I set all that aside, because it only confuses me. I simply and perhaps foolishly hold to this: nothing makes a thing beautiful except the presence and participation of beauty itself, however that participation occurs. I won't commit to the exact mechanism, but I firmly believe that all beautiful things are made beautiful by beauty. This seems the safest answer I can give to myself or anyone else — a principle that will never be overthrown. By beauty, beautiful things become beautiful. Do you agree?'
'I do.'
'And by greatness alone do great things become great and greater things greater, and by smallness do smaller things become smaller?'
'True.'

'So if someone said that A is taller than B by a head, and B shorter than A by a head, you'd refuse to accept it? You'd insist that the greater is greater only by greatness and because of greatness, and the lesser is less only by smallness and because of smallness. You'd want to avoid the absurdity of saying someone is taller by a head — since the head is the same size in both cases, and it would be monstrous to say the taller person is taller because of something small.'
'Yes, I'd be afraid of that,' said Cebes, laughing.

'Similarly, you wouldn't say that ten exceeds eight by two and because of two, but by number and because of number. Or that two cubits exceed one cubit by a half, but rather by magnitude. The same danger applies in all these cases.'
'Very true,' he said.

'And you'd be cautious about saying that adding one to one, or dividing one, is the cause of two? You'd insist that you know of no way anything comes into existence except by participation in its own proper essence. The only cause of two is participation in duality; the way to make one is participation in unity. You'd leave the puzzles of addition and division to wiser heads. Inexperienced as you are, and scared of your own shadow as the saying goes, you'd cling to the safety of your principle. And if someone challenged that principle, you'd ignore them until you'd checked whether the consequences of the principle were consistent. When pressed for an explanation of the principle itself, you'd go higher — to a more fundamental principle — and higher still, until you found solid ground. But you wouldn't confuse the principle with its consequences, as the hair-splitters do. They never care about the truth — they're too busy being clever and pleased with themselves. But you, if you're a philosopher, will do as I say.'
'Absolutely true,' said Simmias and Cebes together.
ECHECRATES: Yes, Phaedo, and rightly so. The clarity of Socrates' reasoning is remarkable, even to someone who wasn't there.
PHAEDO: Certainly, Echecrates — that was the feeling of the whole company.
ECHECRATES: And ours too, hearing your account now. But what came next?

PHAEDO: After all this had been agreed, and they'd accepted that the Forms exist and that particular things participate in them and derive their names from them, Socrates — if I remember correctly — said:
'This is how you speak. And yet when you say Simmias is taller than Socrates and shorter than Phaedo, you're attributing both tallness and shortness to Simmias, aren't you?'
'Yes, I am.'

'But you'd agree that Simmias doesn't really exceed Socrates because he's Simmias — that's not the reason. He exceeds him because of the tallness he happens to have. And he doesn't exceed Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has shortness relative to Simmias's tallness?'
'True.'
'And Simmias isn't shorter than Phaedo because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has tallness relative to Simmias's shortness?'
'That is so.'

'So Simmias is called both tall and short — being between the two. He surpasses one person's shortness with his tallness, and is surpassed by another's tallness with his shortness.' Then he smiled and said: 'I seem to be writing like a legal document. But this is how things really are, isn't it?'
He agreed.

'My point is this: not only will tallness itself never consent to be both tall and short at the same time, but the tallness in us will never admit shortness or consent to be exceeded. One of two things happens: either it retreats and makes way when its opposite — shortness — approaches, or it perishes at the advance of shortness. It will not stand its ground and receive shortness and become something other than what it was. Just as I, having received and admitted shortness while remaining the same person Simmias, am now short. But Tallness itself — being tall — can never become short. Similarly, Shortness in us will never become or be tall. No opposite, while remaining what it is, will simultaneously become or be its own opposite — it either retreats or perishes.'
'I completely agree,' said Cebes.

One of the listeners — I can't remember exactly who — said: 'Wait — didn't we agree earlier that the greater comes from the less, and the less from the greater? That opposites are generated from their opposites? But now you seem to be saying that can never happen!'

Socrates leaned forward and said: 'Brave of you to bring that up. But notice the difference between what we're saying now and what we said before. Before, we were talking about things that have opposite qualities — and we named them after those qualities. Now we're talking about the opposites themselves — the essential qualities whose presence gives things their names. We're saying that these essentials would never accept generation from one another.' Then, looking at Cebes: 'Were you also troubled by this objection?'
'Not this one,' said Cebes. 'But I am troubled by many things.'
'Then let's agree on this general principle: an opposite will never be its own opposite.'
'Absolutely,' he said.
'Now consider whether you'll agree with the next point. Do you call something hot and something cold?'
'Yes.'
'The same as fire and snow?'
'Certainly not.'
'So hot is different from fire, and cold is different from snow?'
'Yes.'
'But I think you'll agree: snow, while remaining snow, will never admit heat — as we said before. When heat approaches, snow either retreats or perishes.'
'Very true.'
'And fire, when cold approaches, either retreats or perishes. It will never accept coldness and still be fire.'
'That is true,' he said.

'Then we find this principle in certain cases: not only is the abstract Form itself entitled to its own name for all time, but there are other things — not the Form itself, but possessing its character whenever they exist — that also claim the Form's name. Here's an example: the odd must always be called odd, mustn't it?'
'Certainly.'

'But is "odd" the only thing that has this name? Or is there something else — not identical to oddness itself, but which must always be called odd because its nature never allows it to be otherwise? I mean the number three, and many other numbers. Consider three: don't you think it must always be called both by its own name and by the name "odd" — even though oddness and three are not the same thing? Three, five, and every alternate number are not oddness itself, but each of them is always odd. Similarly, two, four, and every other alternate number are not evenness itself, but each is always even. Do you agree?'
'Of course,' he said.

'Then mark what I want to show: not only do opposite Forms refuse to admit each other, but things that are not themselves opposites, yet always carry one of a pair of opposites within them — these things also refuse to admit the Form opposite to the one they contain. They either perish or retreat at its approach. We'll say that three would sooner perish than become even while remaining three?'
'Certainly,' said Cebes.
'And yet two and three are not opposites?'
'No, they are not.'
'So it's not only the opposite Forms that don't tolerate each other's approach — there are certain other things that don't tolerate the approach of opposites either.'
'Very true,' he said.
'Shall we define what these are, if we can?'
'Certainly.'
'Would they not be things which compel whatever they occupy to have not only their own nature, but always the nature of some particular opposite as well?'
'What do you mean?'
'What we were just saying. You know that whatever the Form of three occupies must be not only three, but also odd.'
'Certainly.'
'And the Form opposite to the one that produces this effect can never come to that thing.'
'No.'
'And what produced the effect was the Form of oddness?'
'Yes.'
'And the opposite of this is the Form of evenness?'
'Yes.'
'Then the Form of even will never come to three?'
'No.'
'Three has no share in the even?'
'No share.'
'Then three is uneven?'
'Yes.'

'So what I proposed to define — which things, though not themselves opposite to a given thing, still won't admit that opposite — as three, not being the opposite of even, still refuses to admit even, because three always brings along its own opposite — and similarly with two in relation to odd, and fire in relation to cold, and so on — well, let me see if you accept this definition: not only does an opposite not admit its opposite, but anything that brings an opposite along with it into whatever it enters will itself never admit the opposite of what it brings. Let me remind you — it's worth hearing again. Five will never admit the Form of even, nor will ten — the double of five — ever admit the Form of odd. The double is not itself the opposite of odd, but it still won't admit oddness. Nor will three-halves, or other fractions like one-third, admit the Form of the whole — if you follow me and agree.'
'I entirely agree and follow,' he said.

'Then tell me again from the beginning — and don't answer in my exact words, but follow my example. I mean this: beyond the safe answer I first gave, I now see a further kind of safety. If you ask me what makes a body hot, I won't give the safe but ignorant answer "heat" — I'll give a subtler one: "fire." If you ask what makes a body sick, I won't say "sickness" but "fever." If you ask what makes a number odd, I won't say "oddness" but "the number one." And so on. Do you see what I'm driving at?'
'Perfectly,' he said.
'Then tell me: what is it that, when present in a body, makes it alive?'
'The soul,' he said.
'And is this always the case?'
'Of course,' he said.
'Then the soul always brings life to whatever she occupies?'
'Yes, she does.'
'And is there an opposite to life?'
'Yes — death.'
'And the soul, as we've agreed, will never admit the opposite of what she always brings?'
'Absolutely,' replied Cebes.
'Now, what do we call that which doesn't admit the Form of even?'
'The uneven,' he said.
'And what doesn't admit justice, or music?'
'The unjust, and the unmusical,' he said.
'And what do we call that which doesn't admit death?'
'The immortal,' he said.
'And does the soul admit death?'
'No.'
'Then the soul is immortal?' 'Yes.'
'And may we say this has been proven?' 'Completely.'

chapters.title: The Soul Is Immortal
paragraphs: 'Then the soul is immortal?'
'Yes,' he said.
'And may we say this has been proven?'
'Yes, thoroughly proven, Socrates,' he replied.
'Suppose the odd were imperishable — wouldn't three also be imperishable?'
'Of course.'
'And if cold itself were imperishable, when heat came attacking snow, the snow would have to retreat whole and unmelted — it could never perish, but neither could it stay and accept the heat?'
'True,' he said.
'Similarly, if the warm principle were imperishable, fire attacked by cold wouldn't perish or be extinguished — it would simply withdraw unharmed?'
'Certainly,' he said.

'The same logic applies to the immortal: if what is immortal is also imperishable, then the soul cannot perish when attacked by death. As our argument has shown, the soul will never accept death or be dead, any more than three or the odd will accept the even, or fire will accept cold. But someone might object: "Even if the odd can't become even when the even approaches, why can't the odd simply perish and the even take its place?" To that objection, we couldn't respond that the odd is imperishable — we haven't established that. If we had, we could easily argue that when the even approaches, the odd and the number three simply depart. The same argument would hold for fire and heat and anything else.'
'Very true.'
'And the same applies here: if the immortal is also imperishable, then the soul is imperishable as well as immortal. If not, we'll need a different proof of her imperishability.'
'No other proof is needed,' he said. 'If the immortal — being eternal — were still liable to perish, then nothing would be imperishable.'
'Yes,' replied Socrates, 'and everyone would agree that God, the essential form of life, and the immortal in general, can never perish.'
'Everyone — both gods and men, I believe,' he said.
'Since the immortal is indestructible, and the soul is immortal, mustn't the soul also be imperishable?'
'Absolutely.'
'Then when death comes to a person, the mortal part of them may die, but the immortal part withdraws before death and is preserved, safe and sound?'
'True.'
'Then beyond all question, Cebes, the soul is immortal and imperishable, and our souls will truly exist in another world!'

'I'm convinced, Socrates,' said Cebes, 'and I have no further objections. If Simmias or anyone else has something to say, they should speak now — I don't know when there will be another chance for this conversation.'

'I have nothing more to say,' replied Simmias. 'Nor can I see any reason for doubt after what's been said. But I still feel uncertain in my own mind, when I consider the greatness of the subject and the weakness of human understanding.'

'Well said, Simmias,' replied Socrates. 'And I'll add this: even first principles that seem certain should be carefully examined. Once they're satisfactorily established, you may — with a kind of hesitant confidence in human reason — follow the course of the argument wherever it leads. If the path is clear, no further inquiry will be needed.'
'Very true.'

'But then, my friends,' he said, 'if the soul is truly immortal, what care should be taken of her — not just during this thing called life, but for eternity! The danger of neglecting her is terrible. If death were simply the end, the wicked would get a bargain: they'd be happily rid of their body and their evil along with their soul. But since the soul is plainly immortal, there's no escape from evil except through attaining the highest virtue and wisdom. For the soul carries nothing to the next world except its upbringing and education — and these, they say, can greatly benefit or greatly harm the departed at the very beginning of their journey.'

'After death, they say, each person's guardian spirit leads them to a place where the dead are gathered. After judgment, they pass into the underworld, following a guide assigned to lead them from this world to the next. When they've received what they deserve and stayed their allotted time, another guide brings them back after many ages. The road to the other world is not, as Aeschylus says, a single straight path — if it were, no guide would be needed. But there are many forks and winding turns, as I infer from the rites offered at crossroads to the gods below.'

'The wise and orderly soul follows the straight path, aware of her surroundings. But the soul that craved the body — the one I described before, lingering around the corpse and the visible world — is carried away only after long struggle and much suffering by her guardian spirit. When she arrives where the other souls are gathered, if she's impure and has committed terrible deeds — murders or other crimes — every soul flees from her. No one will be her companion or guide. She wanders alone in the extremity of suffering until her appointed time is fulfilled, and then she's carried irresistibly to her fitting dwelling. But every pure and just soul that lived under the guidance of the gods goes to her own proper home.'
'Now the earth has many wonderful regions, and is very different in nature and extent from what geographers believe — at least according to someone whose opinion I trust.'
'What do you mean, Socrates?' said Simmias. 'I've heard many descriptions of the earth, but I'd love to know which one you believe.'

'If I had the skill of Glaucus, Simmias, I'd tell you — though I doubt even Glaucus could prove my tale. And even if I could prove it, my life would end before the proof was complete. But I can describe the earth as I conceive it.'
'That will be enough,' said Simmias.

'Well then,' he said, 'I believe the earth is a sphere in the center of the heavens, needing no air or any other support to hold it up. It's kept in place by the perfect balance of the surrounding heavens and by its own equilibrium. A body in perfect balance, placed at the center of something perfectly uniform, will not tilt in any direction but will remain constant. That is my first conviction.'
'And a correct one,' said Simmias.

'I also believe the earth is enormously vast, and that we who live in the region from the Phasis River to the Pillars of Heracles inhabit only a small fraction of it, clustered around the sea like ants or frogs around a pond. There are many other inhabitants in many similar places elsewhere. For the earth's surface is covered with hollows of various shapes and sizes, into which water, mist, and the lower atmosphere collect. But the true earth is pure and located in the pure heavens where the stars are — what we usually call the ether. What we call earth is just the sediment that has settled into the hollows below. We who live in these hollows are deceived into thinking we live on the surface — just as a creature at the bottom of the sea might imagine the sea is the sky and the surface of the water is the top of the world. They've never risen high enough to see how much purer and more beautiful the world above is. That's exactly our situation: we live in a hollow and think we're on the surface. The air we call sky, in which we think the stars move, is really just the dregs.'

'But the fact is that our weakness prevents us from reaching the surface of the air. If someone could get to the very top — or grow wings like a bird and fly up there — they'd be like a fish poking its head above the water: they'd see a world beyond. If human nature could bear the sight, they'd realize that the upper world is the place of true heaven, true light, and true earth. For our earth, stones, and everything around us is spoiled and corroded, just as everything in the sea is corroded by brine. Nothing noble or perfect grows here — only caves, sand, and endless mud. Our world can't compare with the upper world at all. Of that upper earth beneath the heavens, Simmias, I can tell you a marvelous tale, well worth hearing.'
'We'd love to hear it, Socrates,' replied Simmias.

'The tale is this,' he said. 'Seen from above, the earth looks like one of those twelve-paneled leather balls, decorated with many colors. The colors we painters use here are just pale samples of the colors up there — the whole earth is made of them, and they are far brighter and clearer than ours. There's a purple of extraordinary brilliance, a golden radiance, a white purer than chalk or snow. The earth is composed of these and other colors, more numerous and more beautiful than any human eye has seen. Even the hollows I mentioned, filled with air and water, have their own color and gleam among the others like light amid diversity, so the whole presents a single continuous appearance of endless variety. In this beautiful region, everything that grows — trees, flowers, fruits — is proportionally more beautiful. There are hills with stones smoother, more transparent, and fairer in color than our most prized emeralds, rubies, and jaspers — our gems are just tiny fragments of theirs.'

'The reason is that those stones are pure, not infected or corroded by the foul elements that gather among us, breeding disease in earth, stones, animals, and plants alike. Those are the jewels of the upper earth, which also gleams with gold, silver, and the like — large, abundant, and everywhere visible, making the earth a joy to behold. There are animals and people too — some living in the interior, others dwelling around the air as we dwell around the sea, others on islands surrounded by air near the continent. They use air as we use water, and ether as we use air. Their climate is such that they have no disease and live much longer than we do, with sight, hearing, smell, and all the other senses in far greater perfection — in the same proportion that air is purer than water or ether than air. They have temples where the gods truly dwell, and they hear their voices, receive answers, and converse with them. They see the sun, moon, and stars as they truly are, and their blessedness matches all this.'

'Such is the nature of the whole earth, and of the things around it. There are many regions in the hollows across the globe — some deeper and wider than ours, others deeper with narrower openings, some shallower and wider. They all have numerous openings connecting them, and through these flow vast tides of water, enormous underground rivers that never stop, springs both hot and cold, great fires, and rivers of fire, streams of liquid mud both thin and thick. The regions around which they flow are filled by them. All this is set in motion by an eternal swinging within the earth, caused by a chasm — the greatest of all — that pierces straight through the whole earth. This is what Homer calls the "inmost depth beneath the earth," and what he and other poets call Tartarus.'
'Far off, where is the inmost depth beneath the earth.'

'The swinging is caused by streams flowing in and out of this chasm. They take on the nature of the soil they flow through. Because the water has no fixed bed or bottom, it surges up and down, and the surrounding air does the same, following the water and creating terrifying, irresistible blasts. When the water rushes down, it fills the lower regions of the earth, and when it surges back, it fills the hollows here above. The water flows through underground channels into seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. Then it enters the earth again — some rivers making long circuits through many lands, others shorter journeys — and all eventually fall back into Tartarus, always somewhat lower than where they emerged.'

'Some burst forth on the opposite side of the earth, some on the same side. Some wind around the earth many times like coiled serpents, descending as far as possible before returning to the chasm. The rivers can descend only to the center — beyond that is a precipice in either direction.'

'There are four great rivers. The greatest is Oceanus, flowing around the earth in a circle. Flowing the opposite direction is the Acheron, which passes under the earth through desolate regions into the Acherusian Lake — where the souls of most of the dead go. After waiting their appointed time — longer for some, shorter for others — they're sent back to be born again. The third river emerges between the first two, pours into a vast region of fire, and forms a lake larger than the Mediterranean, boiling with water and mud. Winding through the earth, it reaches the borders of the Acherusian Lake but doesn't mix with its waters. After many coils it plunges into Tartarus at a deeper level. This is Pyriphlegethon, which throws up jets of fire in different parts of the earth.'

'The fourth river emerges on the opposite side and falls into a wild, savage region of dark blue color, like lapis lazuli. This is the River Styx, and it forms the Lake Styx. After receiving strange powers from those waters, it passes underground, winding in the opposite direction, approaching the Acherusian Lake from the other side. Its water mingles with no other — it flows in a circle and falls back into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. The poets call this river Cocytus.'

'Such is the nature of the other world. When the dead arrive at the place their guardian spirit leads them, they first receive judgment based on how they lived. Those who lived neither especially well nor badly go to the Acheron, board whatever vessels they find, and are carried to the lake. There they dwell, are purified of their wrongs, suffer the penalty for what they did to others, and receive rewards for their good deeds — each according to their deserts. But those who are incurable because of the enormity of their crimes — sacrilege, murder, and similar offenses — are hurled into Tartarus and never come out.'

'Those who committed great but not irremediable crimes — who in a moment of anger harmed a parent and then repented for the rest of their lives, or who killed someone under similar circumstances — are plunged into Tartarus for a year. When the year is up, they're cast out — murderers by way of Cocytus, those who harmed parents by Pyriphlegethon — and carried to the Acherusian Lake. There they call out to those they wronged, begging for pity and permission to enter the lake. If they succeed, their suffering ends. If not, they're carried back to Tartarus and then to the rivers again, endlessly, until they win mercy from their victims — for this is the sentence their judges imposed. But those who have lived lives of outstanding holiness are released from this earthly prison and ascend to their pure home above, dwelling in the purer earth. And those among them who have been fully purified by philosophy live henceforth entirely without the body, in dwellings still more beautiful — which I would describe if there were time.'
'Therefore, Simmias, seeing all these things — what ought we not do to gain virtue and wisdom in this life? The prize is beautiful, and the hope is great!'

chapters.title: The Death of Socrates
paragraphs: 'A sensible person shouldn't insist that my description of the soul and her dwelling places is exactly true. But since the soul has been shown to be immortal, they may reasonably believe that something like this is true. The venture of believing is a noble one, and worth comforting ourselves with such words — which is why I've told this long tale. So let a person be of good cheer about their soul, if they've cast aside the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien and harmful, and sought instead the pleasures of knowledge. Let them adorn the soul with her own proper jewels — temperance, justice, courage, nobility, and truth. So adorned, she's ready for the journey to the world below when her time comes. You, Simmias and Cebes, and all others, will depart at some point. But me — as the tragic poet might say — the voice of fate is already calling. Soon I must drink the poison. I think I'd better bathe first, to spare the women the trouble of washing my body after I'm dead.'
When he'd finished speaking, Crito said: 'Do you have any instructions for us, Socrates? Anything about your children, or anything else we can do for you?'

'Nothing special, Crito,' he replied. 'Just what I've always told you: take care of yourselves. That's the greatest service you can render to me and mine and to all of us, whether you promise it now or not. But if you neglect yourselves and refuse to live by the principles I've laid out — not just today, but always — then no amount of promises will help.'
'We'll do our best,' said Crito. 'But how shall we bury you?'

'However you like — but you'll have to catch me first and make sure I don't slip away!' Then, turning to us with a smile: 'I can't convince Crito that I am the Socrates who has been talking and arguing with you. He thinks I'm that other Socrates — the dead body he'll see shortly — and asks how to bury me. Despite everything I've said about going to the joys of the blessed after drinking the poison, my words seem to have had no effect on Crito. So I need you to guarantee him — as he guaranteed me at the trial. He promised the judges I would stay. You must promise him I won't stay, but will go away and depart. Then he'll suffer less at my death and won't grieve when he sees my body being burned or buried. Don't let him say at the funeral, "Here we lay out Socrates," or "Here we follow him to the grave." Such false words are not only wrong in themselves — they infect the soul with evil. Be of good cheer, dear Crito, and say that you are burying my body only. Do with it whatever is customary, and whatever you think best.'

After saying this, he got up and went to another room to bathe. Crito followed; he told us to wait. So we stayed behind, talking about what we'd heard and reflecting on the enormity of our loss. He was like a father being taken from us, and we were about to spend the rest of our lives as orphans. After the bath, his children were brought to him — two young sons and an older one — and the women of his family came too. He spoke with them, gave them some instructions in Crito's presence, then sent them away and returned to us.

It was now near sunset — he'd been inside a long time. He sat down with us again after his bath, but little was said. Soon the prison guard — servant of the Eleven — came in and stood by him. 'Socrates,' he said, 'I know you are the noblest, gentlest, and best person who has ever been in this place. I won't blame you for the angry feelings that other men show me when I tell them to drink the poison, as the authorities require. I'm sure you won't be angry with me — others are to blame, not I. So farewell, and try to bear what must be as easily as you can — you know why I've come.' Then, bursting into tears, he turned and went out.

Socrates looked at him and said: 'I return your good wishes, and I'll do as you ask.' Then, turning to us: 'How kind the man is! The whole time I've been here, he's visited me often and talked with me, and been as good to me as anyone could be. And now look how generously he grieves for me. We must do as he says, Crito. Bring the cup, if the poison is ready. If not, have the attendant prepare it.'

'But Socrates,' said Crito, 'the sun is still on the hilltops. I know many men wait until late — after the announcement has been made, they eat, drink, and enjoy the company of those they love. Don't hurry — there's still time.'

'Yes, Crito, the people you describe are right to do that — they think they gain something by the delay. But I'm right not to follow their example. I wouldn't gain anything by drinking the poison a little later. I'd only look foolish in my own eyes, clinging to a life that's already forfeit. Please do as I ask, and don't refuse me.'

Crito signaled to the servant standing nearby. The servant went out, was gone for some time, and returned with the guard carrying the cup of poison. 'You,' said Socrates, 'you're experienced in these things — tell me what to do.' The man answered: 'Just walk around until your legs feel heavy, then lie down. The poison will do its work.' He handed the cup to Socrates, who — in the easiest and gentlest manner, Echecrates, without the slightest fear or change of color or expression, looking the man full in the eyes as was his way — took the cup and said: 'May I pour a libation from this cup to any god? Or is that not allowed?' The man answered: 'We prepare only enough for a single dose, Socrates.' 'I understand,' he said. 'But I may and must pray to the gods that my journey from this world to the next be fortunate. So be it — that is my prayer.' Then, raising the cup to his lips, he drank the poison with perfect calm and cheerfulness. Until that moment, most of us had managed to hold back our tears. But when we saw him drinking — saw that he'd finished — we could control ourselves no longer. In spite of myself, my tears were streaming down. I covered my face and wept — not for him, but for myself, at the thought of losing such a friend.

I wasn't the first to break down. Crito had already gotten up, unable to hold back his tears. And Apollodorus, who had been weeping the whole time, now burst into such loud, passionate sobs that he broke the heart of everyone present. Only Socrates remained calm. 'What is this strange outcry?' he said. 'I sent the women away precisely to prevent this kind of thing. I've been told that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, and have patience.' We were ashamed when we heard him, and held back our tears. He walked about until, as he said, his legs grew heavy, and then he lay on his back, as instructed. The man who had given him the poison checked his feet and legs from time to time. After a while he pressed his foot hard and asked if he could feel it. 'No,' Socrates said. Then the man pressed his legs, and so upward, showing us that he was growing cold and stiff. Socrates felt it himself and said: 'When the cold reaches my heart, that will be the end.' He was growing cold around the midsection when he uncovered his face — he had drawn the cloth over himself — and spoke his last words: 'Crito, I owe a rooster to Asclepius. Will you remember to pay the debt?' 'It shall be paid,' said Crito. 'Is there anything else?' There was no answer. After a moment or two, there was a slight movement. The attendants uncovered him. His eyes were fixed. Crito closed his eyes and mouth.
Such was the end of our friend, Echecrates — a man of whom I may truly say: of all the men of his time that I have known, he was the wisest, the most just, and the best.
